Let us talk about people. How do you evaluate a finance team, and what do you actually look at?
Three things. Does the number arrive on the day it was promised. Is it right the first time. And does the business go to that person before a decision, or after it.
The third one is not in any system I know of. So how do you measure it?
I do not measure it, I ask. I ask the commercial director who he calls when he is building a pitch. If my controller's name has not come up in a year, that is the performance review right there.
And hours? Some of your peers put availability quite high on that list.
Never. If somebody needs twelve hours to do nine hours of work, the problem is bandwidth or process, and both of those are mine, not theirs.
Good. Then the other one. If you joined us in September, what would your first twelve months look like?

By the end of month one I will have met all four direct reports and sat in on one close. By the end of the quarter I will have decided which of the three systems we keep. And this time next year we will be closing in five days rather than nine.
Three things: on the promised day, right the first time, and asked before the decision.
The third one I cannot measure, so I ask the business instead.

How do I evaluate a finance team. Three things, and they are always the same three. One, does the number arrive on the day it was promised. Two, is it right the first time, because a number that has to be corrected costs more credibility than a number that is late. And three, and this is the one that separates a good controller from a good business partner, does the business go to that person for advice before the decision, or after it. The first two I can measure from a calendar and an error log. The third one I cannot measure at all, so I ask. I ask the commercial director who he calls when he is putting a pitch together, and if my controller's name does not come up in a year, that tells me everything. And notice what is not on that list. Hours. I have never once evaluated anybody on hours, and I would not join a company that did.

The twelve month question is the one candidates prepare least and it is the one we care most about, because it is the only part of the interview that is about us rather than about them. A weak answer is a list of intentions. I will assess the team, I will review the processes, I will build relationships. Everybody says that and it tells me nothing. A strong answer has dates in it. By the end of the first month I will have met all four direct reports individually and I will have sat in on one close. By the end of the quarter I will have decided which of the three systems we keep. This time next year we will be closing in five days rather than nine. That last sentence is the one I write down, because it is a commitment, it is measurable, and it means the person has already understood what is broken here.
